title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Pineal region tumors are rare lesions, representing about 1% of intracranial tumors in adults and up to 8% in children. The diversity of these tumors reflects the variety of cell types within the pineal gland and the numerous structures located nearby. These tumors may originate from the pineal parenchyma, represent germ cell neoplasms, arise from adjacent tissues, or develop as metastases from distant sites. Given their location, they frequently present with obstructive hydrocephalus or dorsal midbrain compression, requiring timely recognition and management.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity provides a comprehensive review of the evaluation, classification, and management of pineal gland tumors. Learners explore diagnostic strategies, treatment algorithms, and prognostic factors, while also gaining insight into the critical role of the interprofessional team, including clinicians, advanced practitioners, nurses, pharmacists, and allied specialists, in optimizing patient-centered care, improving safety, and enhancing outcomes for individuals with these rare intracranial tumors.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Introduction
content: The pineal gland is a small endocrine structure, measuring 10 to 14 mm in length, located in the midline of the brain at the superior aspect of the posterior margin of the third ventricle. On coronal imaging, the gland lies below the splenium of the corpus callosum and above and posterior to the tectum of the midbrain. [1] The principal function of this gland is the secretion of melatonin, a hormone that regulates circadian rhythms. The gland receives environmental light-dark cycle information and provides feedback to the central nervous system, thereby contributing to the regulation of biological rhythms. [2]

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Introduction
content: The principal cells of the pineal gland are pinealocytes, which constitute the pineal parenchyma. Multiple pathologies are associated with this region due to the variety of cell types and structures adjacent to the pineal gland. Tumors of the pineal gland are classified into 3 subgroups—pineal parenchyma tumors, germ cell tumors, and lesions originating from adjacent structures. [1] Other lesions encountered in this area include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, pineal cysts, meningiomas, arachnoid cysts, ependymomas, chemodectomas, epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, metastasis, aneurysm of the vein of Galen, arteriovenous malformation, and cysticercosis. title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Introduction
content: Differentiating tumors of the pineal region relies on integrating clinical presentation, imaging characteristics, tumor markers, and histopathology. Although many tumors present with overlapping symptoms such as hydrocephalus and Parinaud's syndrome, radiologic features, calcification patterns, and serum or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) markers such as alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), help narrow the differential. Definitive diagnosis requires histological evaluation to guide management.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Etiology
content: The etiology of pineal gland tumors is determined by their histopathological classification. These tumors are broadly divided into 2 major groups—pineal parenchymal tumors and germ cell tumors. Pineal parenchymal tumors Pineocytoma Pineal parenchymal tumor with intermediate differentiation Pineoblastoma Papillary tumor of the pineal region Germ cell tumors Germinomatous germ cell tumors Pineal germinoma Nongerminomatous germ cell tumors Choriocarcinoma Embryonal carcinoma Yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tract tumor) Immature teratoma Mature teratoma

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Epidemiology
content: Tumors of the pineal region are rare, comprising approximately 1% of all intracranial tumors in adults, but up to 8% of intracranial tumors in children. The heterogeneity of neoplasms in this region results in wide variation in their clinical characteristics and epidemiology. The World Health Organization is one form of classification often used (see Table. 2016 World Health Organization Classification). [4] Abbreviations: CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; AFP, alpha-fetoprotein; hCG, human chorionic gonadotropin; WHO, World Health Organization; M:F, Male:Female.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Pathophysiology
content: The pineal gland develops during the seventh week of gestation. [20] In humans, its principal function is the production of melatonin, a hormone that regulates circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles. The gland is also involved in regulating puberty and reproductive functions.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Pathophysiology
content: Tumors of the pineal region are diverse in origin due to the proximity to multiple anatomical structures. The pineal gland commonly sequesters embryonic germ cells, which explains why germ cell tumors represent some of the most common pathologies in this location. [21]

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Pathophysiology
content: Germ cell tumors typically occur sporadically. [22] However, they have been associated with certain genetic and syndromic conditions, including Klinefelter syndrome, Down syndrome, and neurofibromatosis type 1. title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Histopathology
content: The histopathology of pineal region tumors is highly heterogeneous, reflecting the diverse cellular origins within and around the gland. Tumors may arise from pineal parenchymal cells, germ cells, or adjacent structures, each with distinct morphologic and immunohistochemical profiles. Accurate histopathological classification is essential for guiding prognosis and therapeutic strategies.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Histopathology -- Pineocytoma
content: Pineocytomas are comprised of small cells resembling normal pinealocytes, typically arranged in sheets. [26] A characteristic histological feature is the presence of pineocytomatous pseudorosettes, which are absent in normal, healthy pineal gland tissue. [4] [6] Pineocytomas lack a well-formed blood-brain barrier, resulting in vivid contrast enhancement on imaging. [27] Immunohistochemical staining demonstrates positivity for synaptophysin, neurofilament protein, and neuron-specific enolase. Other neuronal markers, including Tau protein, chromogranin-A, and 5-hydroxytryptamine, may show variable positivity, while neuronal nuclei staining is characteristically negative.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Histopathology -- Pineal Parenchymal Tumors with Intermediate Differentiation
content: These tumors display 2 characteristic microscopic growth patterns—lobulated or diffuse. [4] The lobulated pattern shows poorly defined lobules separated by large fibrous blood vessels. In contrast, the diffuse pattern resembles that of oligodendrogliomas or central neurocytomas, and the large pineocytomatous rosettes typical of pineocytomas are absent. Immunohistochemical staining typically demonstrates positivity for synaptophysin, variable expression of neurofilament protein, and negativity for neuronal nuclei.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Histopathology -- Papillary Tumor of the Pineal Region
content: Papillary tumors of the pineal region exhibit a variable morphology, ranging from solid to predominantly papillary growth patterns. The histological appearance of these tumors often resembles that of ependymomas and may include ependymal rosettes. [28] Foci of necrosis are sometimes observed within the tumor. [4] [7] [28] Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for cytokeratins, such as AE1/3, CAM5.2, KL1, and CK18; S100; vimentin; transthyretin; neuron-specific enolase; and microtubule-associated protein 2. Glial fibrillary acidic protein demonstrates variable expression.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Histopathology -- Pineoblastoma
content: Pineoblastomas are composed of densely packed small, round blue cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Histologically, Homer Wright and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes are occasionally observed. [4] Tumor necrosis is common, and the mitotic rate is typically high. [4] Immunohistochemically, pineoblastomas demonstrate positivity for synaptophysin and SMARCB1, whereas other neuronal markers, including neuron-specific enolase, neurofilament protein, and chromogranin-A, show variable expression.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Histopathology -- Germinoma
content: Germinomas originate from primordial germ cells and share morphological features with their gonadal counterparts. The tumor cells exhibit large nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and dense lymphocytic infiltration is frequently present. Immunohistochemically, the cells are positive for placental alkaline phosphatase. [10] CSF analysis may reveal elevated placental alkaline phosphatase and β-hCG. [10]

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- History and Physical
content: The clinical presentation of pineal region tumors is mainly related to obstructive hydrocephalus and compression of the tectum or dorsal midbrain. [29] Consequently, regardless of the pathology, the physical examination findings are similar across the different tumor types. Hydrocephalus: History: Headache, nausea, vomiting, failure to thrive, macrocephaly, blurry vision, lethargy, drowsiness, or coma. Examination: Cushing triad: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations Bilateral optic nerve swelling or papilledema Bilateral sixth nerve palsy Compression of the tectum or dorsal midbrain (Parinaud syndrome): History: Difficulty walking up stairs and diplopia

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation
content: The evaluation of pineal region tumors requires a multimodal approach that integrates clinical, radiologic, and laboratory findings. Neuroimaging, particularly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast, is central to identifying the tumor and its relationship to adjacent structures. In contrast, CSF fluid analysis and serum tumor markers help differentiate germ cell tumors from other pineal lesions. Hisopathological confirmation remains essential for definitive diagnosis and treatment planning.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Evaluation
content: Serum tumor markers are obtained when specific tumors are suspected, particularly those of the germ cell type. The most commonly assessed markers include AFP, β-hCG, and placental alkaline phosphatase. [30] These markers provide important diagnostic and prognostic information and may help distinguish between germinomatous and nongerminatous tumors.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Evaluation
content: CSF analysis can be performed via lumbar puncture, provided there is no obstructive hydrocephalus, or during endoscopic procedures. CSF evaluation helps diagnose many tumors of the pineal region and can provide complementary information to serum markers and imaging findings (see Image. Tumor Markers).

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Brain MRI with and without gadolinium enhancement is the gold standard for evaluating pineal region tumors. When MRI is not available, alternative imaging modalities such as head computed tomographic (CT) scan, angiography, and, in infants, cranial ultrasound can play a role in the assessment of pineal region mass lesions. Normal neuroimaging findings of the pineal gland: CT scan: Calcification of the pineal gland is a common finding in adults but is typically absent in children younger than 5. The prevalence of this calcification peaks around the age of 30. [31] MRI: On MRI, the pineal gland demonstrates signal intensity similar to that of gray matter and appears as a small nodule of tissue located in the posterior aspect of the third ventricle. Because the gland lacks a blood-brain barrier, it shows avid enhancement with gadolinium. Calcifications are also frequently visualized on MRI. [20]

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Brain MRI shows homogeneous enhancement in pineal region tumors, except in cases with heterogeneous cellularity. Dense tumors, such as pineoblastomas and germinomas, often exhibit restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging. In contrast, pineal cysts typically lack enhancement and are characterized by a thin wall. Therefore, the presence of a thick lesion wall excludes the diagnosis of a cyst.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Calcifications are more readily identified on head CT and can sometimes assist in establishing an accurate diagnosis. Pineal parenchymal tumors such as pineocytoma and pineoblastomas typically demonstrate peripheral calcifications, whereas germ cell tumors tend to encompass the calcified pineal tissue.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Many tumors of the pineal region may spread locally or seed distantly. Therefore, a complete spinal MRI is often recommended as a part of the initial evaluation. Evidence of local invasion or remote dissemination carries important prognostic implications and can significantly alter both initial management and the selection of adjuvant therapy.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Evaluation -- Prognosis Indicators
content: Findings associated with a worse prognosis include local invasion, CSF seeding, and extensive peritumoral edema. These features can significantly impact survival outcomes and influence the treatment approach. Local invasion is most often observed in pineoblastomas and many germ cell tumors. The presence of local invasion reflects aggressive biological behavior and can complicate surgical resection. CSF seeding is another indicator of poor prognosis. Pineoblastomas most frequently demonstrate distal dissemination, whereas germinomas are more likely to exhibit proximal seeding.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management
content: Following established treatment algorithms is essential for the evaluation of pineal region tumors. These protocols ensure both accurate diagnosis and appropriate management. If hydrocephalus is absent: Obtain tumor markers in serum and CSF If positive, treatment should proceed based on the most likely pathology If negative, tissue diagnosis is required Biopsy (stereotactic, endoscopic, open) Resection (guided by radiographic or preliminary pathology findings) The confirmed pathology determines final management If hydrocephalus is present: CSF diversion should be performed, with endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) being the preferred approach. Always attempt an endoscopic biopsy when performing an ETV Final management is based on pathology

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy
content: ETV is performed by fenestrating the floor of the third ventricle, thereby creating a passage between the third ventricle and the prepontine cistern. In most cases, a right frontal burr hole is made anterior to Kocher's point, and the neuroendoscope is advanced through the brain parenchyma into the ipsilateral lateral ventricle. From there, the floor of the third ventricle near the tuber cinereum is fenestrated and expanded to permit adequate CSF flow. If abnormal tissue is visualized, a biopsy is obtained from the posterior aspect of the third ventricle. Should ETV fail, definitive treatment involves placement of a ventricular shunt.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy
content: The ETV success score is calculated using 3 variables—age, cause of hydrocephalus, and prior ventricular shunt placement. Each variable is assigned a success percentage, which is added to yield a total score ranging from 0% to 90% (see Table. Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy Success Score). [32]

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: The underlying pathology guides definitive treatment of pineal region tumors. Surgical resection is the mainstay for all pineal parenchymal tumors, mature teratomas, and for residual disease following chemotherapy and radiotherapy, in what is termed second-look surgery. [33]

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: Radiotherapy is primarily used in the treatment of germinomas but is generally reserved for patients older than 3. In younger patients, alternative approaches are preferred to minimize long-term neurocognitive effects.
contents: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment. Radiotherapy is primarily used in the treatment of germinomas but is generally reserved for patients older than 3. In younger patients, alternative approaches are preferred to minimize long-term neurocognitive effects.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: Chemotherapy combined with radiotherapy represents the standard for most other pineal region tumors. This approach is indicated for all nongerminomatous germ cell tumors and for germinomatous germ cell tumors in children younger than 3. Adjuvant chemotherapy with radiotherapy is also recommended for all tumors, except pineocytomas and mature teratomas, when complete resection has been achieved.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: The surgical approach to the pineal region is determined based on the tumor's location and the surgeon's preference. The paramedian infratentorial supracerebellar approach is considered the most flexible option for resection of the most pineal region tumors, except for large lesions that extend laterally and inferiorly. [34] This technique involves a left-sided suboccipital craniotomy, which protects the torcula and the typically more dominant right-sided veins and dural sinuses, including the transverse sinus.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: The midline infratentorial supracerebellar approach has traditionally been used to expose pineal region tumors. [35] This technique is performed via a bilateral midline suboccipital craniotomy but is limited by restricted lateral and inferior visualization due to the tentorial angle and the obstructive apex of the culmen. In addition, nearly all midline bridging vermian veins must be sacrificed.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: The occipital transtentorial approach is beneficial for large pineal region tumors that extend laterally and inferiorly. [36] [37] [38] This technique is performed through a unilateral occipital craniotomy. Limitations include challenges with anatomic orientation, the need to divide the tentorium, and the risk of homonymous hemianopia resulting from occipital lobe retraction.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Treatment / Management -- Treatment
content: Screening of the entire neuroaxis is essential in all patients with pineal region tumors. Prognosis and treatment vary dramatically depending on whether CSF dissemination is present. Distant CSF seeding, except germinoma, and drop metastases are associated with poor outcomes. Comprehensive screening requires MRI of the brain, as well as the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine, with and without contrast. The role of prophylactic spinal radiotherapy remains controversial.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of pineal region tumors is broad, reflecting the variety of neoplastic and nonneoplastic lesions that may arise in this location. Careful consideration of clinical presentation, imaging characteristics, and histopathology is essential to distinguish these entities and guide appropriate management. Cystic nonneoplastic lesions: Pineal cysts Cavum veli interpositum Arachnoid cyst Pineal parenchymal tumors: Pineocytoma Pineal parenchymal tumor with intermediate differentiation Pineoblastoma Papillary tumor of the pineal region Germ cell tumors: Pineal germinoma Embryonal carcinoma Choriocarcinoma Teratoma (mature/immature) Yolk sac tumor Tumors also encountered in the pineal region: Astrocytoma Meningioma Cerebral metastases Pineal gland metastases Vascular lesions: Vein of Galen aneurysm/malformation Internal cerebral vein thrombosis

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of pineal region tumors varies widely (see Table. Prognosis Summary of Pineal Region Tumors) and is closely linked to tumor histology, extent of resection, and presence of CSF dissemination. Advances in neuroimaging, microsurgical techniques, and multimodal therapy have improved survival outcomes, although specific aggressive subtypes continue to carry a poor prognosis. Abbreviation: CSF, cerebrospinal fluid.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Complications
content: Complications of pineal region tumors arise from both the tumor itself and its treatment, including neurological deficits, endocrine dysfunction, and treatment-related morbidity, all of which can significantly affect long-term outcomes and quality of life. title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Pineal region tumors may recur even after long disease-free intervals, underscoring the need for prolonged follow-up. Patients with cerebral CSF shunts require lifelong monitoring to detect shunt-related complications. As prognosis and treatment are closely tied to tumor histology, patients and families must receive counseling about the specific tumor type and the potential need for adjuvant therapy.

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key facts to keep in mind about gland tumors include the following: Geminoma is the most common pineal tumor; it is highly radiosensitive and has an excellent prognosis. Pineoblastoma is an aggressive tumor that occurs in children and is linked to bilateral retinoblastoma (trilateral retinoblastoma). Classic presentation includes hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome (upward gaze palsy, light-near dissociation). AFP and β-hCG are key markers (elevated in nongerminomatous germ cell tumors; β-hCG sometimes in germinomas). MRI is the gold standard. Calcification pattern on MRI Peripheral=parenchymal tumor Engulfed=germ cell tumor

title: Pineal Gland Cancer -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal management of pineal region tumors requires an interprofessional approach that emphasizes not only clinical expertise but also effective communication, shared responsibility, and ethical collaboration. Clinicians and advanced practitioners provide diagnostic accuracy, surgical and medical management, and evidence-based decision-making. Nurses play a critical role in perioperative and postoperative care, patient education, and monitoring for complications, ensuring safety and continuity of care. Pharmacists contribute through precise chemotherapy and supportive medication management, reducing risks of adverse effects and improving treatment adherence.
